source_user: Design a small controlled experiment for continuous batching. Case variant 1: include one concrete mechanism and one boundary condition.
source_assistant: Continuous batching admits and retires requests at iteration boundaries so completed sequences do not hold a static batch slot.
corrected_answer: Hypothesis: under a fixed model and hardware, continuous batching improves decode goodput or tail latency for a variable-length workload at a specified arrival rate, but not necessarily prefill latency. Use the same weights, tokenizer, precision, runtime, concurrency cap, request-length distribution, and arrival trace for a static-batch baseline and the continuous scheduler. The mechanism to test is iteration-boundary retirement of completed sequences followed by admission of queued requests; instrument scheduler events, active slots, queue time, KV allocation, and prefill/decode times. Sweep load and prompt/output lengths, warm up, repeat with randomized order, and report median/p95/p99 TTFT, inter-token latency, completion time, tokens/s or goodput, peak memory, errors, and output correctness with uncertainty. A boundary is available KV capacity and scheduler policy: requests may queue, be paged, or fail near memory limits, so do not generalize beyond tested regimes.
risks: Unequal arrival traces or length distributions can make the baseline comparison invalid.
KV pressure, queueing, and implementation-specific admission behavior may reverse the observed benefit.
evidence_required: Versioned model, runtime, hardware, precision, and scheduler settings.
Identical request trace, prompt/output length distributions, concurrency and memory limits.
Per-request latency, phase timing, scheduler/KV telemetry, errors, correctness, and repeated-run uncertainty.

source_user: Design a small controlled experiment for continuous batching. Case variant 2: include one concrete mechanism and one boundary condition.
source_assistant: Continuous batching admits and retires requests at iteration boundaries so completed sequences do not hold a static batch slot.
corrected_answer: Compare a static batching policy with continuous batching on the same inference server. Hold weights, hardware, software, precision, maximum context, concurrency, and a replayed arrival/length trace constant; vary only the scheduler policy. In decode, record when a finished sequence releases its slot and when a waiting request enters the next iteration—that is the mechanism. Measure warm-up-excluded TTFT, inter-token latency, p95/p99 completion latency, throughput/goodput, queueing, active batch size, KV-cache usage, peak memory, failures, and exact output agreement. Repeat each condition and sweep offered load and length skew. One boundary condition is that prefill may use a separate batching path and the benefit can disappear or become harmful when KV memory is saturated; report those regimes separately rather than claiming a universal speedup.
risks: Changing both admission policy and workload invalidates causal attribution.
Average throughput alone can hide queueing and tail-latency regressions.
evidence_required: Controlled scheduler-only change and reproducible arrival replay.
Phase-separated request metrics and active-slot/KV telemetry.
Load sweep, repetitions, correctness checks, and confidence intervals or comparable uncertainty summaries.

source_user: Design a small controlled experiment for continuous batching. Case variant 3: include one concrete mechanism and one boundary condition.
source_assistant: Continuous batching admits and retires requests at iteration boundaries so completed sequences do not hold a static batch slot.
corrected_answer: Define a factorially small study with scheduler {static, continuous} and load {low, medium, near saturation}; keep model, device, precision, runtime, prompt/output lengths, and client behavior fixed. Replay the same trace, discard warm-up, and randomize run order. The concrete mechanism is replacement at a decode iteration boundary: completion retires a request and admission fills the freed slot without waiting for the whole batch to finish. Collect per-request TTFT, decode inter-token latency, completion latency, queue delay, throughput/goodput, active-slot occupancy, KV-cache bytes, peak device memory, errors, and token-level correctness. A boundary is that continuous scheduling does not remove prefill cost or guarantee capacity: long contexts and KV fragmentation can force waiting, eviction, or rejection. Interpret results only within the tested load and length distribution.
risks: Near-saturation runs can confound scheduler effects with throttling or OOM behavior.
Occupancy is only a proxy and does not establish better user-visible service.
evidence_required: Pre-registered factors, fixed trace, and exact resource limits.
Scheduler, queue, KV, memory, latency, throughput, failure, and correctness logs.
Repeated trials across load and length skew with uncertainty reported.

source_user: Design a small controlled experiment for continuous batching. Case variant 4: include one concrete mechanism and one boundary condition.
source_assistant: Continuous batching admits and retires requests at iteration boundaries so completed sequences do not hold a static batch slot.
corrected_answer: Use a matched replay benchmark rather than comparing separate random requests. For each scheduler, run the same fixed model and hardware configuration over identical prompt and generation lengths, with a documented concurrency and arrival rate. Verify that continuous batching performs its claimed mechanism—retire completed decode sequences and admit waiting ones only at defined iteration boundaries—by tracing membership over time. Measure step/iteration duration, active requests, queue delay, TTFT, inter-token and p99 latency, goodput, KV allocation/fragmentation, peak memory, failures, and output correctness; repeat enough times to estimate variation and include cold/warm behavior separately. The boundary is phase and capacity: a scheduler optimized for decode may not improve prefill, and a full KV pool may cause queueing or rejection. Do not mix metrics or infer causation from utilization alone.
risks: Mixing prefill and decode metrics can create a false performance conclusion.
Tracing or instrumentation overhead may perturb short requests.
evidence_required: Matched replay and versioned configuration.
Verified scheduler membership trace and phase-separated timing.
Memory/KV, errors, correctness, and repeated-run variance with instrumentation overhead noted.

source_user: Design a small controlled experiment for continuous batching. Case variant 5: include one concrete mechanism and one boundary condition.
source_assistant: Continuous batching admits and retires requests at iteration boundaries so completed sequences do not hold a static batch slot.
corrected_answer: Test the claim with a two-policy, three-load experiment: static batch versus continuous batching at low, moderate, and high offered load. Keep model weights, device, runtime, precision, context/output-length distributions, concurrency cap, and arrival sequence fixed; warm up and repeat each cell. Inspect scheduler traces to confirm that a completed request is retired and a queued request admitted at the next decode iteration, rather than assuming the mechanism. Report TTFT, inter-token and p99 completion latency, queue time, generated-token goodput, utilization, active-slot occupancy, KV/peak memory, errors, and correctness. A boundary is resource and workload dependence: at low load there may be no slot to refill, while under KV saturation continuous admission can increase waiting or failures; prefill and decode must be analyzed separately. State uncertainty and avoid universal speedup claims.
risks: A single load point cannot support a general scheduler claim.
Admission can improve occupancy while worsening fairness or tail latency.
evidence_required: Fixed replay, load sweep, and scheduler event trace.
Per-request latency/goodput/fairness and phase-specific metrics.
KV/memory/failure/correctness telemetry and replicated uncertainty estimates.

source_user: Write a concise runbook entry for an engineer investigating continuous batching. Case variant 2: include one concrete mechanism and one boundary condition.
source_assistant: Continuous batching admits and retires requests at iteration boundaries so completed sequences do not hold a static batch slot.
corrected_answer: Runbook: (1) Record model/runtime/device/precision, scheduler policy, concurrency, arrival trace, prompt/output lengths, and KV/memory limits. (2) Separate prefill from decode and establish a static-batch or equivalent baseline on the same replay. (3) Trace each decode iteration: confirm completed requests retire and queued requests are admitted at the iteration boundary; check queue delay, slot occupancy, KV allocation, and errors. (4) Compare per-request TTFT, inter-token/p99 latency, completion time, throughput or goodput, peak memory, and output correctness across repeated low-to-high-load runs. (5) If latency regresses, inspect queueing, length skew, synchronization, KV fragmentation, and admission limits. Boundary: continuous batching is a runtime policy and may help variable-length decode but does not automatically improve prefill or training, and full KV capacity can cause waiting or rejection. Preserve logs and report measured facts separately from estimates.
risks: Treating a scheduler label as proof of behavior can conceal implementation differences.
A baseline with different client or length distributions is not diagnostic.
evidence_required: Versioned configuration and matched baseline replay.
Iteration membership, queue, KV, memory, failure, and correctness telemetry.
Repeated phase-separated latency and goodput measurements.

source_user: Write a concise runbook entry for an engineer investigating continuous batching. Case variant 4: include one concrete mechanism and one boundary condition.
source_assistant: Continuous batching admits and retires requests at iteration boundaries so completed sequences do not hold a static batch slot.
corrected_answer: Runbook: first freeze the configuration and replayable workload, then verify whether the server actually retires finished decode requests and fills those slots at iteration boundaries. Capture request arrival, admission, queue, prefill, decode iterations, KV pages/bytes, memory, and errors. Compare against a static policy using identical requests and report TTFT, inter-token latency, p95/p99 completion latency, queueing, goodput, active-slot occupancy, and correctness; repeat runs and separate warm-up. Investigate long-tail regressions through length skew, queue fairness, synchronization, cache fragmentation, and capacity thresholds. Boundary: the mechanism applies to a particular runtime and decode path; prefill may follow another scheduler, and near KV capacity admission may block, page, or fail. Do not claim benefit without matched measurements.
risks: Instrumentation can miss hidden scheduler queues or add overhead.
Mean latency can hide starvation and p99 regressions.
evidence_required: Scheduler event trace and exact workload replay.
Phase-separated per-request latency, queue/fairness, goodput, memory/KV, error, and correctness data.
Repeated runs with instrumentation and warm-up treatment documented.

source_user: Write a concise runbook entry for an engineer investigating continuous batching. Case variant 5: include one concrete mechanism and one boundary condition.
source_assistant: Continuous batching admits and retires requests at iteration boundaries so completed sequences do not hold a static batch slot.
corrected_answer: Runbook: document the model, runtime, hardware, precision, scheduler, limits, and fixed arrival/length trace. Establish a matched static-batch baseline. In a trace, verify the mechanism—when a decode request finishes, it is retired at an iteration boundary and a waiting request can occupy the freed slot—and correlate that event with queue time, active slots, and KV usage. Measure TTFT, inter-token and tail latency, completion time, goodput, peak memory, failures, and output correctness over repeated loads, with prefill and decode reported separately. If results are mixed, check length skew, synchronization, fairness, KV fragmentation, and admission thresholds. Boundary: continuous batching cannot guarantee lower latency; at low load there may be no refill opportunity, and at KV saturation it may queue or reject requests. Keep hypotheses distinct from measured observations.
risks: A scheduler may implement admission differently from its name or documentation.
Capacity and fairness effects can dominate any utilization improvement.
evidence_required: Versioned runtime configuration and replayed matched workload.
Direct admission/retirement trace plus queue, phase, KV, memory, failure, and correctness metrics.
Repeated load/length-sweep results with uncertainty.

source_user: Define tensor parallelism and explain one reason it matters in LLM infrastructure. Case variant 1: include one concrete mechanism and one boundary condition.
source_assistant: Tensor parallelism shards computation within layers and introduces collective communication; the best degree depends on memory, topology, batch, and communication cost.
corrected_answer: Tensor parallelism (TP) partitions a layer's tensors and associated computation across multiple devices, then uses collectives such as all-reduce or all-gather so the next operation sees the required partial or reconstructed results. It matters because sharding can reduce per-device parameter and activation memory and enable a model or batch that does not fit on one device, at the cost of communication and synchronization on the critical path. The concrete mechanism is partitioned matrix multiplication followed by a topology-dependent collective. A boundary is that more TP ranks are not automatically faster: small batches, short sequences, insufficient interconnect bandwidth, imbalance, replication choices, or communication contention can erase the benefit, and exact collectives depend on the implementation. Specify layer shapes, batch/sequence units, precision, devices/topology, and measure compute, collective time, memory, throughput, and latency before generalizing.
risks: TP memory savings and communication behavior vary by layer partition and runtime.
Comparing devices or ranks without fixing topology and workload can misattribute performance.
evidence_required: Model layer shapes, TP degree, precision, device type/count, topology, and runtime configuration.
Per-layer compute/collective timings and peak memory.
Matched batch/sequence workload with latency, throughput, and correctness checks.

source_user: Define tensor parallelism and explain one reason it matters in LLM infrastructure. Case variant 2: include one concrete mechanism and one boundary condition.
source_assistant: Tensor parallelism shards computation within layers and introduces collective communication; the best degree depends on memory, topology, batch, and communication cost.
corrected_answer: Tensor parallelism splits selected layer weights or intermediate activations across devices so each device computes a shard of a matrix operation; a collective communication step combines or exchanges those shards before dependent computation. This can make a large layer fit within per-device memory and may increase usable model scale, but it does not eliminate total memory or compute and adds synchronization. For example, a sharded linear layer produces partial outputs that are reduced or gathered according to the parallel layout. The boundary condition is workload and interconnect: with small matrices or low batch, communication latency and imbalance may dominate, while a fast fabric and sufficiently large work may amortize it. Record TP degree, topology, model dimensions, batch/sequence lengths, precision, and runtime; measure peak memory, collective/compute time, end-to-end latency, throughput, and output equivalence.
risks: The exact shard and collective pattern is implementation-dependent.
Memory capacity is not the same as end-to-end performance or scaling efficiency.
evidence_required: Partition specification and layer dimensions.
Hardware topology, communication timings, memory accounting, and runtime version.
Matched workload, scaling measurements, and numerical/output correctness validation.
